432:### Process findings
436:1. **The relayed request again.** The coordinator launched in the turn of his message "Boot light.", and every agent read it as "the only user voice in this task … this request wins". Proposed (mine), as at climb batch 27: call `Workflow` only from a `send_later` check-in turn, or in a turn whose latest human message is the go itself; and have the shared brief say that a relayed text that names no part of the batch is out of its scope. Home: the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "The go"; the script's shared brief.
437:2. **The coordinator's JVM-running agents beside the run and the gate.** The literals study (08:04 to 08:39) ran 39 JVM calls beside the gate's distance stage and suites, so F-240's distance figure was taken at load 3.42. The row 364 probe (07:21 to 07:45) ran 35 beside skeptics S and H, the judge and the gather's start. Both were his requests, and each could have waited for the push at 08:46. Proposed (mine): from the gather's start to the commit stage's end, the coordinator starts no agent that runs a JVM; and the gate's machine block names the JVMs that run when a timed stage starts. Home: `references/batch.md`, "While it runs"; the script's gate brief.
438:3. **The backup's six-hour gap, and the first planner lost.** No turn of the main session ended from 16:55 to the loss, since no check-in was armed while the first planner ran. So the backup took no snapshot, and the planner's work after 16:55:14 was lost uncommitted. The relaunch armed one and committed as it went. Proposed (mine): arm a check-in whenever an agent runs with no turn of the session's due (`cloud-container`, `references/hooks.md`, already says that check-ins end turns). Home: `references/batch.md` or `delegating.md`, before a planner's launch.
439:4. **The shallow clone after a rebuild.** Eight agents could not reach the team's history (section 7, point 7). Proposed (mine): after a rebuild, unshallow the main clone (`git fetch --unshallow origin`, not tried here) and check `git rev-parse --verify a874948ac`; until then, `records.md` names the fallback, the file's copyright header. Home: `cloud-container`'s `references/container-loss.md`; `fortress-repo`'s `records.md`, "The repository's history".
440:5. **A foreground call past the cache's life.** Skeptic H's four `timeout 120` runs of a hanging program in one call took 490 s and cost a refill of 204K. Proposed (mine): the skeptic brief has a program that may hang run in the background with one `timeout`, its wait alone. Home: the script's skeptic brief.
441:6. **The cost estimate.** 6.65M against 4.6M. The skeptics' base was climb batch 27's, taken on a full disk; this batch's skeptics averaged 357K. Proposed (mine): about 0.35M a skeptic where the rung edits Java and the library, and about 0.9 hours a rung at two agents at a time. Home: the manual's "Preparing a batch record".
442:7. **`compiler.md` past 30,000 characters** (30,491). Two agents' `cat` was saved to a file and read again (about 25K together). Proposed (mine): trim it below 30,000, or split "The checker's time" off. Home: the skill writer.
443:8. **The shared brief misstates the skill on `revival-changes.md`.** It says to read it whole "which its SKILL.md says every task needs"; `SKILL.md` exempts a task that only runs a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a commit. The gate and the commit stage read it (about 19K). Proposed (mine): the preamble names the roles that read it. Home: the script.
444:9. **P-148's `pass` run when the second pass changes nothing.** It measures the change's commit again (section 7, point 2). Proposed (mine): step 4 runs `pass` only where the second pass changed code, and otherwise cites `change`. Home: `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", step 4.
445:10. **`spend.py`'s folders.** A record-landing's headless writer sessions live in the landing worktree's project folder, which climb batch 27's review left out. Proposed (mine): `spend.py`'s header names `-home-user-fortress-landing-*`; and for a span before a rebuild, the review reads the backup by each transcript's last record, as this one did. Home: `tools/spend.py`.
446:11. **`File`, `Reader` and `System` are outside the distance's fourteen.** S's moved bindings and R's rewritten components are checked by no gate stage on the merged tree. P-58 holds for the bindings in `FortressLibrary`, and S ran its own probe. Proposed (mine): the distance's list gains `System`, `File` and `Reader`, microGPT's imports (F-290), or the gate runs S's `checkApi` probe. Home: `tools/distance/run.sh` and the manual's "Gate"; this is the coordinator's call, since P-39 keeps the stage report-only either way.
447:12. **A test api's jar in the main tree's caches.** The gather's compiled test runs left `TraitTableApiTraitApi.jar` in `default_repository/caches/`, which the gate copied for the ladder; nothing compared differently. Proposed (mine): the gather's `junit.sh` runs use a private caches folder. Home: the script's gather brief.
449:### Misses, by kind
495:## Part 3. For the skill writer
500:1. **`fortress-repo`, `references/interpreter.md:98`**, the carriers' list, which lacks the reader trait. Ground: F-332; P-164. Proposed, beside the writer's item: "`JavaBufferedReader`, the library's reader trait, in `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressBufferedReader`, through a private native object below it;".
501:2. **`references/compiler.md:76`**, "So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches.", which lacks the array slots. Ground: F-333; P-169. Proposed: "So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches, and, through `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`, each element of the one library's compiled array store by its array and index."
502:3. **`SKILL.md:123`**, "Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes". The same addition holds, once the compiled path reads the one library (until the switch-over, compiled programs use the prelude's arrays). Ground: F-333.
505:4. **`references/interpreter.md:128`**, "So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`." Since H, `Utility.makeFortressException(name, msg)` raises the exception with the message on the compiled path, and walk raises the library's object without it. Ground: F-336; row 930 closed; item 384. Proposed, after the sentence: "With a message, `makeFortressException(name, msg)`: the compiled path's exception carries it; walk's carries none (review-queue item 384)."
506:5. **`references/compiler.md`, its size**, 30,491 characters, past the tool's 30,000 (process finding 7).
507:6. **`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"**, which has no sentence for P-161's checked getters: `ZZ` converts out only by its five getters, each `as…` raises `IntegerOverflow`, the `bitsAs…` keep the bits, and the low-bits names are on every type where they apply. For the orientation update; F-331 brings it.
508:7. **`references/records.md`, "The repository's history"**, whose `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` fails in a shallow clone (process finding 4); and **`cloud-container`, `references/container-loss.md`**, which does not name the shallow clone. The second goes to the coordinator's own skill writer, since the record-landing workflow's writer brings `fortress-repo` alone.

584:2. **FACTS and the ledger:** findings A to C.
585:3. **The script, between batches:** process findings 1 to 12.

623d6912d
623d6912d
24:- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25:
26:Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`, as in `simpleIntArith.java`.
27:
28:The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
54:- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
55:
56:It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
57:
58:The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
62:## What the code generator does
63:
64:- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
65:- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
66:- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
67:- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
68:
69:      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
70:
71:## The runtime
72:
74:- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.
75:
76:## Natives
77:
78:`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
79:
80:A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
81:
82:- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
96:- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
97:
98:The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
99:
100:The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

46:- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47:- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48:- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49:
50:A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
51:
52:- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53:- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54:- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
104:- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
105:- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
106:- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
107:- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
108:- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
109:  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
110:  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).
111:
112:## The checker's gaps
113:
114:- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
115:- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
116:  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
145:## Before an edit
146:
147:Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
148:
149:- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
150:
159:## Testing an edit here
160:
161:- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
162:
163:      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
172:## The checker's time
173:
174:This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
175:
176:The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
177:
178:The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
198:
199:A node's hash starts from its class's name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks or a union's members, moves only where the change itself moves it. Such a move is a difference: keep the old order, or report the difference, as for any other.
200:
201:`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node, so one long walker method slows the whole checker. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
202:
203:The timing is a smoke test. It is there to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
204:
205:If you change the checker:
206:
207:1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
208:2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
209:
210:       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
211:       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
212:
213:3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
214:4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
215:5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
216:6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
217:
218:To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
219:
220:    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'

Meaning: under walk no conversion goes through a coercion, and `narrow(z)` of a `ZZ` finds no declaration (write `z.asZZ32`); until the switch-over the compiled prelude has 8 of the 25 getters and no `big` (row 349). == explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:97
- P-161 **The integer conversions: checked `as…` getters that raise `IntegerOverflow` on every integer type, `bitsAs…` getters for the bit pattern, today's names as the low-bits forms, and `ZZ`'s `narrow` and `widen` deleted.** On each of `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64` and `ZZ`, the getters `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` and `asZZ` raise `IntegerOverflow` where the value does not fit: of the 25, 5 are identities, 7 equal the coercions and 13 can raise. The four fixed widths have the compiler prelude's `bitsAs…` getters. `narrow`, `widen`, `unsigned`, `signed` and `big` keep the low bits, each declared on every type where it applies, so that no call reaches one through a coercion. `ZZ`'s conversions out are its five getters; the callers of its `narrow` and `widen` (`Library/Format.fss`, `Library/QuickCheck.fss`, the demo `sudoku.fss`, the test `XXXZZNarrowRungP`) move onto `.asZZ32` or `.asZZ64` with their values unchanged. The specification states the getters and names beside `narrow`'s sentence in `basic-integers.tex`, drops `ZZ` from it, and gives an Appendix I entry. P-72 (`narrow` keeps the low 32 bits on the fixed widths), P-73 (fixed-width arithmetic raises) and P-74 (an exact conversion is implicit) stand. So `z.asZZ64` raises for a `ZZ` too large, and `unsigned` of a negative value keeps the low bits, with `x.asNN32` or `x.asNN64` as its check. Why: the team's later work, Steele's prelude, made `asZZ32` raise in 2011 and named the bits `bitsAs…` in 2012; the specification's general sentence says that an integer result that overflows throws `IntegerOverflow`; a plain name that checks beside a name that tells its loss is Swift's and Julia's pattern; and `ZZ`'s two are wrong code: its `widen` can narrow, and turns 2^63 negative.

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). A message can follow as a second argument, as in `nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53`, which raises `FailCalled`. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero`, `IntegerOverflow` and `FailCalled`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: `throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero")` (`compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java`). The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and `StaticNativeApp` raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as `DivisionByZero` and `IntegerOverflow`. `DIV`, `REM` and `MOD` by zero on `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64` raise `DivisionByZero` in this way, on both paths. So no division, remainder or modulus by zero on these types ends the run. A `catch` sees no other Java exception, so any other Java exception of a native, a glue class's included, ends the run.

**An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161).** To convert a value, write a getter, as `x.asZZ32`: `asZZ32`, `asZZ64`, `asNN32`, `asNN64` or `asZZ`. It keeps the value or raises `IntegerOverflow`. The low-bits functions `narrow`, `widen`, `signed`, `unsigned` and `big` keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's `(int)` does. On the fixed-width types, `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32` and `NN64`, `narrow` and `widen` give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, `signed` and `unsigned` the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and `big` a `ZZ`. So `narrow` of a `ZZ64` outside `ZZ32`'s range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as `widen` of a `ZZ64`. `ZZ` has only `big`, so for a `ZZ` value `z`, `narrow(z)` finds no declaration: write `z.asZZ32`. Each `bitsAs…` getter equals `unsigned` or `signed`, as `bitsAsNN32` of a `ZZ32`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: `asZZ` on each fixed-width type, `asZZ32` on `ZZ32` and `ZZ64`, `asNN32` on `NN32`, and `asNN64` on `NN64`. It has no `big`, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as `narrow` of a `ZZ64` (row 349).

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method also counts for it. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.

.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md:35:: Run of the batch workflow (`references/batch.md`) that changes the tree in several rungs and lands their merged work. The record names each one a climb batch, by number, with its folder `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/`.
3:The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.
55:- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
78:- The rungs, their skeptics and their judges work in their own worktrees, and do not read the main tree. The gather and the stages after it work there, and the gather needs `git status --porcelain` to print nothing. So until the gather starts, commit in the main tree as usual, by named paths, and push at once. From the gather's start until the batch's push, change nothing there. Keep `origin/main` at or behind the main tree's head, or git refuses the commit stage's push. So push `main` from no other tree. From the main tree, push nothing that the batch committed: the commit stage pushes it.
103:4. After the post-batch review is committed, run the record-landing workflow (`explorations/coordinator/tools/record-landing/README.md`). It brings FACTS, POSITIONS, INDEX, PLAN and the review queue in line with the landing. Its Land stage, the step that lands its commits on `main`, also pushes them. Then it runs the orientation workflow in update mode itself, on the entries that the landing added or changed. The orientation workflow writes new text for each section of `fortress-repo`'s `revival-changes.md` that these entries touch. Next, the workflow has the skill writer install the sections that the orientation judge accepts. The writer also brings in line the sentences of `fortress-repo`'s `SKILL.md` and other parts that the landing's changes to FACTS and POSITIONS made false, and no others. A new rule, or a change of a rule's meaning, is not made in the workflow: the writer lists it for you in its reports, `writer-1.md` and `writer-2.md` in `explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/skills/`. After the workflow ends, judge each such rule on its merits: what it protects against what it costs, its ground, and whether the skill already covers it. Then take it or drop it. Give the rules that you take to your own skill writer. They land after their cold read and the writer's fixes (`references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method"). Name the rules that you dropped, with their reasons, in one line of the message that sends the curator the one line for the page of `fortress-repo` changes (below). The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

P-148                                                      POSITIONS.md:61, The one library and the compiled checker  [904 bytes]
- P-148 **The checker's speed comes right after its correctness in priority: a rung that changes the compiled checker also makes the change fast.** The rung times the checker before and after its change. It first makes the change correct. Then, in the same rung, it makes the new code fast, without changing which programs the checker accepts or refuses. So no optimization is left to be done by hand after the landing. Why: the checker must stay usable as it grows. Some slowdown is fine, but new checks have made it orders of magnitude slower, so that the checker ran past the time limit of the batch gate's count stage, and rungs could not land. The timing is a smoke test: one run of each tree, to catch a slowdown of several times; a small difference is noise. Change 50 · revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”The object fix works because nothing can extend an object

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

revival-changes.md, “Dispatch and overloading”, line 24, the Meet Rule paragraph, its two sentences on the fix; the rest did not change

Declare the trait excludes { Number }, or make it exclude arrays, excludes { HasRank }. Or declare the + in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, but because no other type can extend it.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the fix stays, and one word now gives its reason. The sentence gives a fix for a program's trait whose own + overlaps the library's +: declare the + in an object. It said that an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, “but” no other type can extend it. With “but”, the last clause read as a cost of the fix. The specification gives it as the fix's reason: an object's type cannot be extended, so it excludes every type that is not its supertype. So no type can be both the object and a Number. The text now says “because”. The orientation update's own cold read raised it, and its judge said to install it.

Change 51 · revival-changes.md, “Numbers”An integer converts by a checked getter or by a low-bits function

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

revival-changes.md, “Numbers”, line 93, a new rule after the rule on coercions

An integer converts to another integer type by a checked getter or by a low-bits function (P-161). To convert a value, write a getter, as x.asZZ32: asZZ32, asZZ64, asNN32, asNN64 or asZZ. It keeps the value or raises IntegerOverflow. The low-bits functions narrow, widen, signed, unsigned and big keep the low bits and never raise, as Java's (int) does. On the fixed-width types, ZZ32, ZZ64, NN32 and NN64, narrow and widen give the 32-bit and the 64-bit type of the same sign, signed and unsigned the signed and the unsigned type of the same width, and big a ZZ. So narrow of a ZZ64 outside ZZ32's range wraps silently. In the interpreter's library, each fixed-width type has all five functions, and one that keeps the type returns the value, as widen of a ZZ64. ZZ has only big, so for a ZZ value z, narrow(z) finds no declaration: write z.asZZ32. Each bitsAs… getter equals unsigned or signed, as bitsAsNN32 of a ZZ32. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude has only these getters: asZZ on each fixed-width type, asZZ32 on ZZ32 and ZZ64, asNN32 on NN32, and asNN64 on NN64. It has no big, and of the low-bits functions only those that change the type, as narrow of a ZZ64 (row 349).

Why. A new rule. By your decision, each integer type has checked getters, which raise IntegerOverflow where the value does not fit, and the batch made it so. The functions narrow, widen, signed, unsigned and big stay, as the forms that keep the low bits and never raise, and ZZ lost its narrow and widen. The part had no rule on converting one integer type into another. A worker would have written narrow where a value out of range must raise, or called narrow on a ZZ, which now finds no declaration, or written in a compiled test a getter that the compiler's prelude lacks. The rule says which to write, what each gives, and what the prelude has until the switch-over. The orientation update's own checks shaped its sentences on the prelude. After the skill's cold read, “all five” and “of the five”, which could mean the getters or the functions, now say “functions”. “Under walk” became “In the interpreter's library”, since the fact is the library's, and the checker reads that library too. The call form x.asZZ32 now stands at the start, so that a worker does not write asZZ32(x) after the next rule's asFloat(x). The text names the fixed-width types and gives each low-bits function's result type, which the skill writer checked in the library, and it says that z is a ZZ. It says that each bitsAs… getter equals unsigned or signed, so that a worker need not choose between them. And it lists the prelude's eight getters, where the first wording gave only their number.

Change 52 · interpreter.md, “Natives”A helper's raise can carry a message

New text; struck through, what went; underlined, what came in

interpreter.md, “Natives”, line 128, the paragraph on how a helper raises an exception, up to its sentence on the exceptions to raise; the sentences after it did not change

A helper runs on both paths, so it raises an exception as compiled code does: throw Utility.makeFortressException("fortress.CompilerBuiltin$DivisionByZero") (compiler/runtimeValues/Utility.java). A message can follow as a second argument, as in nativeHelpers/runtime.java:53, which raises FailCalled. The string names the compiler's prelude's class for the exception. Under walk, that class does not load, and StaticNativeApp raises the interpreter's library's object of the same name in its place, without the message. So raise from a helper only an exception that both libraries declare as an object, as DivisionByZero and IntegerOverflow, IntegerOverflow and FailCalled.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the paragraph now states a form that the batch made work. Since the batch, a helper can raise an exception with a message, given as a second argument. On the compiled path the exception carries the message, so that FailCalled, FileNotFoundException and IOFailure raised by a helper reach a catch. Under walk the exception still comes without the message. The paragraph showed only the call without a message, so a worker would not have known that a helper can pass one, or would have asserted the message under walk. After the cold read, the sentence names the line that raises FailCalled with a message, so that a worker need not search for an example. And FailCalled joins the exceptions that a helper may raise, since both libraries declare it as an object: a worker could not tell before whether it may.

Change 53 · compiler.md, “The runtime”The compiled transaction tracks array elements from the switch-over

New text; underlined, what came in; nothing went

compiler.md, “The runtime”, line 74, its second bullet, on the transaction: two sentences added at its end

  • The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks BaseTask.inATransaction() (runtimeSystem/). Inside an atomic block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java calls the transaction's methods TXReadSlot and TXWriteSlot. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with ArrayStoreJUTest, beside it.

Why. Neither a new rule nor a change of a rule's meaning: the bullet now states a fact that the batch made. The batch put the elements of the one library's arrays into a Java store, FortressArrayStore, and the compiled transaction tracks each element of that store, keyed by its array and its index. The bullet said only that the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. Compiled programs use the compiler's prelude's arrays until the switch-over, so the elements are tracked only from then on. After the cold read, the text says that TXReadSlot and TXWriteSlot are methods of the transaction, where a worker could not tell whether they were classes or methods. It also says that walk does not run the class, since walk keeps these arrays in a store of its own, and that an edit of the class is tested with the unit test beside it. A worker would otherwise not have known which path's tests reach the class.

Change 55 · records.md, “The repository's history”What to do in a shallow clone

records.md, “The repository's history”, line 116, a new bullet after the one on the history commands
